name: Mariagenspiel (Mariage)
description: Mariagenspiel is the historical ancestor of the vast 'Marriage' family of card games, which includes global hits like Sixty-Six, Schnapsen, Pinochle, and Belote. Its name literally means 'Marriage Game', referring to the core mechanic: earning bonus points by holding and declaring a King and Queen of the same suit. It is a trick-taking game where players must balance the pursuit of card points with the opportunistic timing of their marriages.

history.origins: First appearing in French and German gaming books in the early 18th century (c. 1715). It set the standard for bonus-point declarations.
timeline: 1800s: Evolved into 'Sixty-Six' (66) in Germany and 'MariÃ¡Å¡' in Central Europe.
1900s: The simplified versions (like 66) become more popular than the complex parent game.
Present: Rarely played in its original 18th-century form, but its spirit lives on in dozens of regional national games.
history.cultural: Used as the baseline for teaching trick-taking logic in the 19th-century Austro-Hungarian classrooms.
history.evolution: The game pioneered the 'Trick-and-Draw' phase, allowing players to build their hands while the stock is still full.

setup.players: Two players. The game is played by two people; each receives six cards at the start. One card is turned face-up for trump (the seven of trumps may be exchanged for it). While the stock lasts, after each trick both players draw to refill to six cards.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 6 cards. One card is flipped to determine the Trump suit.

rules.objective: Be the first to reach a target score (usually 66 or 100 points) through tricks and marriages.
rules.gameplay:
1. **Phase 1**: Players play tricks and then draw a card to stay at 6. No obligation to follow suit.
2. **Phase 2**: Once the stock is empty, suit-following and trumping rules apply.
3. **Victory**: A player can declare a marriage only after winning their first trick.
keyRules: Phase 1: no obligation to follow suit; after each trick both players draw to refill to 6.
Phase 2 (stock empty): must follow suit or trump if unable; no more draws or marriage declarations.
Marriage (K+Q same suit): 20 pts plain, 40 in trumps; declare only after winning a trick.
66 card points win the deal; last trick worth 10 extra. Trump 7 may rob the turn-up.

strategy.basic: Don't play your King or Queen if they are part of a marriage until you have at least one trick won. You cannot declare the bonus points unless you have captured cards to put the bonus into.
strategy.intermediate: Stock Management: In the first phase, discard your 7s and 8s to the table to 'fish' for Aces and 10s from the deck. The first phase is about hand optimization, not point capture.
strategy.advanced: The 'Closing' Bluff: If you suspect you have 66 points in hand (cards + declared marriages), you can 'close' the game. This stops all drawing. If you were right, you win; if not, your opponent gets a massive point bonus. Use this to stop an opponent who just drew a dangerous card.
tips: Keep the Ten of Trumps safe. It is worth 10 points and is second only to the Ace in power.
Last Trick: Winning the final trick is worth a bonus (usually 10 points). In a close game, this is often the tie-breaker.
